description: We're Dallas Atlas, a team of two from Carrollton, TX. We are building Analog Hunter, the first way to crowdsource analog data on the Earth from key Moon and Mars Sites.
summary:
Analog Hunter is a web game and research tool that searches Earth for places that resemble sites on the Moon and Mars. Our model compares every part of Earth’s land with a target site across 10 factors, including slope, roughness, relief, cold extremes, temperature swing, ice and dust, using open NASA and partner-agency satellite data.

In the Analog Hunter game, players get 5 sites from NASA’s Artemis III south-polar landing regions and Mars, and have 30 seconds to drop a pin where Earth matches best. They score for how close the match is, plus a bonus for good picks few others chose.

The Analog Atlas, built for researchers, uses the same model to show a heatmap and ranked list of the best analogs worldwide. Users pick one of 4 jobs, adjust 10 weights and export results as CSV or GeoJSON. A findings card shows which factors match, where the comparison breaks down, and which jobs a place suits best.

The challenge asks for new, well-described analogs, not just famous ones. Analog Hunter searches the whole planet, explains every match and its limits, and ties each result to a real exploration task. Strong, rare player picks become community candidates for researchers to review.

Artemis and Mars missions depend on testing on Earth first, yet today’s analog sites cover few terrains. Analog Hunter gives researchers a transparent, customizable way to find new ones while inviting the entire world to help search.
details:
What it does and how it works

Analog Hunter compares every land and ice cell on a half-degree grid of Earth with a real Moon or Mars landing region. For each cell, it calculates a distance: a weighted sum of squared differences across 10 surface and climate features. Each feature is scaled by how much it varies across Earth’s land. When a target value is something Earth can never reach, such as a lunar night, the cell is scored against the closest value Earth reaches. A cell’s validity is its percentile among all land and ice cells, so 100 means the best match on Earth.

The project has two modes built on the same math:

  • Analog Hunter (the game): every player gets the same five sites each day and has 30 seconds per site to drop a pin. Players score on match quality, plus a rarity bonus for strong picks that few other players chose.
  • Analog Atlas (for researchers): users choose the landing region, the mission and the feature weights, see a heatmap and the ranked top sites, and export them as CSV or GeoJSON. Selecting a cell opens a findings note. It shows the mission that cell fits best, the rock type from the GLiM global lithology map, and any nearby cave, impact crater or extremophile site.

Benefits

Analog Hunter makes analog research easy to use. The heatmap, ranked list and findings note show which places on Earth match a Moon or Mars site and why, so researchers can compare places without building their own data pipeline. The game adds something no single team can do alone: thousands of players exploring the whole planet. Their strong, rare picks show up on the Atlas as community candidates. These point to small, overlooked places beyond the famous analogs, where the satellite grid alone might miss what makes a place useful.

Intended impact

The goal is to help a mission team find a place on Earth where it can test wheels, seals, instruments or field geology before flight. The game also brings the public into that search. Strong picks far from known sites become community candidates that researchers can review.

Tools and technologies

  • Front end: React and Vite, with the 3D globe drawn in CesiumJS over NASA GIBS imagery.
  • Data processing: Python, NumPy and rasterio.
  • Leaderboards and picks: Supabase.
  • Sound: synthesized in the browser with the Web Audio API, so no audio files are used.
  • Data: open NASA and partner-agency datasets, listed in our references.

Creativity

Most analog studies are done by small expert teams looking at a handful of well-known sites. Analog Hunter turns that search into a daily game that invites the whole world to help. Anyone with a browser gets the same five real NASA landing sites, drops a pin in 30 seconds, and earns more points for good picks no one else thought of. Rewarding players for going where nobody has looked points the game straight at the goal of the challenge: finding new analogs. Play and research use the same scoring model, so every player who shares their result helps grow a global, crowdsourced map for scientists.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about limits: gravity, vacuum and radiation never match on Earth, and every findings note says so. Values Earth can’t reach are scored against the closest value Earth reaches.
  • Scale: the grid is coarse, so small features are context only and never scored.
  • Data status: the Earth side uses real satellite data for every land and ice cell: MODIS for temperature, vegetation, brightness, snow and ice, and dust, and the Copernicus DEM for slope, roughness and relief. Moon slope and temperature, and Mars slope and relief, are measured from NASA data files. Ice, surface brightness and Mars temperature on the Moon and Mars side are still estimates. Rock type is a label, not a scored feature. The app states these limits.
  • Accessibility: a mobile-first layout, a short tutorial, plain-language results, and a science view for anyone who wants the details.
  • Openness and privacy: open data, open-source code, sound made in code, and nickname-only play with no accounts.
